stem: Starting from |00>, a three-gate sequence prepares a two-qubit product state whose `plot_bloch_multivector` rendering is shown below. Which sequence prepared it?

stem.alt: Two Bloch spheres side by side, titled 'qubit 0' and 'qubit 1'. The qubit 0 sphere has its arrow lying in the equatorial plane pointing along the negative y axis; the qubit 1 sphere has its arrow pointing straight down at the |1> pole.

explanation.correct: `h(0)` takes qubit 0 to |+>, whose Bloch arrow points along +x. `sdg` is a -90 degree rotation about z, so it swings that equatorial arrow from +x to -y — the direction drawn on the first sphere. `x(1)` flips qubit 1 from |0> to |1>, which is the arrow pointing at the south pole of the second sphere. The state stays a product state, so each sphere carries a full-length arrow.

distractors.A: S versus S-dagger: `s` rotates by +90 degrees about z, sending the +x arrow to +y — the opposite equatorial direction from the one drawn.
distractors.B: Order matters: applying `sdg` to |0> only adds a phase, so the arrow is still at the north pole when `h` runs, and the sequence leaves qubit 0 pointing along +x rather than -y.
distractors.C: Qubit-index swap: this prepares the equatorial arrow on qubit 1 and the flipped arrow on qubit 0, which is the mirror image of the sphere titles in the figure.
distractors.E: `z` on |0> is a phase only, so qubit 1 would still point at the north pole; nothing in this sequence flips it to |1>.

provenance.notes: Stem-figure item: the Bloch drawing is the question, the options are candidate gate sequences. figures/s1-q051/generate.py asserts that the rendered state has exactly the Bloch vectors the proof uses as TARGET.
